questions.question: Which molecule (A to D) can rotate the plane of plane-polarised light? A H2NCH2COOH, B HOCH2CH2COOH, C ClCH2C(CH3)(Cl)COOH, D H2NC(CH3)2COOH.
questions.answer: C - ClCH2C(CH3)(Cl)COOH (it has a chiral carbon)
steps: Only chiral molecules, which are non-superimposable mirror images, rotate plane-polarised light.
A chiral molecule needs a carbon atom bonded to four different groups.
A (glycine) has CH2 with two H atoms, so there is no chiral carbon.
B (HOCH2CH2COOH) has no carbon bonded to four different groups.
D has a central carbon with two identical CH3 groups, so it is achiral.
C has a central carbon bonded to CH3, Cl, CH2Cl and COOH, all different, so it is chiral and optically active.

questions.question: A single optical isomer of a bromoalkane RBr reacts with OH- by an SN1 mechanism to give a racemic alcohol. Which type of bromoalkane is most likely? A primary only, B secondary only, C tertiary only, D primary, secondary or tertiary.
steps: A racemic product forms when OH- attacks a planar intermediate from either face with equal probability.
SN1 proceeds through a carbocation intermediate, which is planar.
A primary bromoalkane cannot be chiral at the C-Br carbon, since CH2Br has two H atoms, so it cannot be a single optical isomer.
A chiral C-Br carbon needs three different alkyl groups plus Br, which fits a tertiary bromoalkane.
Tertiary carbocations are the most stable, so SN1 is most favoured for tertiary bromoalkanes.
Therefore RBr is most likely a tertiary bromoalkane only.

questions.question: A single enantiomer of 2-iodobutane reacts with sodium hydroxide and the product is a mixture of enantiomers. Why? A it is a nucleophilic substitution, B it proceeds via a negatively charged transition state, C it proceeds via a carbocation intermediate, D its rate depends on the concentration of 2-iodobutane.
questions.answer: C - the reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate
steps: Forming a mixture of enantiomers from one enantiomer is racemisation.
Racemisation needs a planar, achiral intermediate that can be attacked from either face.
A carbocation intermediate has a planar sp2 carbon, as in an SN1 mechanism.
OH- attacks the planar carbocation from either side with equal probability.
Equal amounts of two mirror-image products form, giving a racemic mixture.
A is true of all substitutions but does not explain racemisation; B and D do not explain it either.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term stereoisomer.
questions.answer: Stereoisomers have the same structural formula (atoms bonded in the same order) but a different arrangement of the atoms in space.
steps: Stereoisomers have the same molecular formula.
They have the same structural formula, so the atoms are bonded in the same order.
They differ only in the spatial (3D) arrangement of their atoms.
Examples are optical isomers (enantiomers) and geometric (E/Z) isomers.

questions.question: A single stereoisomer of 2-bromobutane is hydrolysed. Explain the stereochemistry of the product.
questions.answer: The product is a single enantiomer (optically active, not racemic) with inverted configuration compared with the reactant.
steps: Hydrolysis of 2-bromobutane by OH- follows an SN2 mechanism in one concerted step.
OH- attacks the carbon from the side opposite the C-Br bond (backside attack).
As the C-Br bond breaks, the other three groups flip like an umbrella, giving inversion of configuration (Walden inversion).
Only one enantiomer of the reactant is present, so only one enantiomer of the product forms.
There is no planar intermediate, so no racemisation occurs and the product is optically active.
